Newly hatched Bynoe geckos emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs at a snout-to-vent length of 2.0 cm [Lb = 2.0 cm], a modest size characteristic of this lineage. The incubation period required to reach this hatching event is 81.6 days [ab = 81.6 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a duration that is relatively protracted compared to some other gekkonids and reflects the species' adaptation to cooler, arid-zone thermal regimes. The wet weight of these neonates is correspondingly low, calculated from the length-mass relationship typical of the species to be approximately 0.17 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.17 grams], a value that underscores their dependence on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days post-hatching. This initial mass provides the nutritional foundation for the period of rapid early growth that follows.

Juvenile Bynoe geckos undergo a sustained period of somatic development before reaching the size threshold associated with sexual maturation. Field studies indicate that individuals attain a snout-to-vent length of 4.2 cm [Lp = 4.2 cm] at the onset of puberty, a value derived from the smallest recorded gravid female in the population, though this may represent a slight underestimate of the true mean. The corresponding wet weight at this pubertal stage is approximately 1.55 grams [Wwp = approximately 1.55 grams], calculated using the established length-weight allometry. This significant increase from birth mass reflects the accumulation of lipid stores and skeletal development necessary to support the energetic demands of gamete production and, ultimately, oviposition. Reaching this size and mass typically requires several months of active foraging during the warmer seasons.

Under optimal thermal conditions, the maximum reproductive rate of Bynoe geckos has been quantified. When maintained at 29 °C [T = 29 °C], females can produce, on average, 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 5 eggs per clutch] and produce approximately 2 to 3 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 to 3 clutches per year]. This figure represents the upper limit of annual fecundity observed under controlled laboratory conditions, reflecting a trade-off between egg size, which is relatively large for a gecko of this body dimension, and the frequency of oviposition events. The rate is constrained by the time required for vitellogenesis and egg shelling, as well as by the availability of sufficient resources to sustain repeated reproductive bouts. In the wild, realized fecundity is likely lower due to seasonal variation in prey abundance and the energetic costs of thermoregulation, particularly during cooler months.

Another critical milestone in the life history of this gecko is the onset of first reproduction. Data from longitudinal field studies indicate that females begin to breed at an age of approximately 204.6 days after hatching [tR = approximately 204.6 days after hatching] when reared under a thermal regime of 29 °C [T = 29 °C], representing the sum of the incubation period and a subsequent post-hatching growth phase. This age at first breeding is a key demographic parameter that influences population growth rates and generation times. Furthermore, the ultimate or asymptotic snout-to-vent length that adults can achieve is around 5.0 cm [Li = around 5.0 cm], representing the maximum size attained after growth has largely ceased. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for an individual of this size is roughly 2.69 grams [Wwi = roughly 2.69 grams], marking the final adult body mass.

Longevity in Bynoe geckos is notable for its length relative to body size, a feature often associated with a slow life-history pace in arid-zone reptiles. Records from mark-recapture studies, including a notable recapture by Kearney, Moritz, and Roberts of an individual at Paynes Find Station that had been marked 15 years earlier as an adult, indicate a maximum lifespan in the wild of approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] at an ambient temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This exceptional survival underscores the species' ability to persist through extended periods of environmental unpredictability. Such longevity, combined with delayed maturation and modest annual fecundity, positions Heteronotia binoei EA6 as a classic bet-hedging strategist, reliant on adult survival to buffer against sporadic recruitment success in the variable Australian arid zone.
